query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A short-duration, low-temperature rapid annealing treatment applied immediately after deformation enhances atomic bonding and relieves residual interfacial stresses in eutectic high‐entropy alloys, thereby reducing microcrack initiation at dual-phase lamellar boundaries and simultaneously improving both tensile ductility and strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high‐entropy alloys with dual‐phase lamellar colonies (e.g., soft fcc and hard B2 phases) containing numerous internal boundaries that serve as microcrack initiation sites during room-temperature tensile deformation.
generation.intervention: Apply a rapid, low‐temperature post-deformation annealing treatment with a high heating rate and very short duration, targeting localized diffusion along the lamellar interfaces.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile deformation conditions. The annealing step must be carefully controlled (narrow temperature window and short treatment time) to promote interfacial diffusion without significant grain coarsening or alteration of the established lamellar architecture.
generation.structural_mediator: Improved interfacial cohesion resulting from enhanced atomic bonding and stress relaxation at the lamellar boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The rapid annealing treatment facilitates localized diffusion along the phase interfaces, relieving residual stresses and healing incipient defects that normally act as microcrack nucleation sites. This selective enhancement of boundary cohesion helps maintain the dual-phase architecture essential for high strength while reducing crack propagation, thereby boosting ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under room-temperature tensile loading, the annealed samples are predicted to exhibit a statistically significant reduction in microcrack density, improved ductility (greater elongation), and maintained or slightly enhanced tensile strength compared to samples processed solely by conventional deformation methods.
generation.baseline: Eutectic high‐entropy alloys processed by conventional deformation methods, which typically display high strength but limited ductility due to microcrack formation at weak lamellar interfaces.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected only when the annealing parameters (temperature, heating rate, and duration) are optimized; excessive time or temperature may lead to grain coarsening and deterioration of the finely tuned lamellar structure, negating the improvements in mechanical properties.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvements in strength and ductility remain uncertain and may vary with the exact alloy composition and initial microstructural state; further parameter optimization is required to define the ideal treatment window.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same eutectic high‐entropy alloy: one set processed by conventional deformation methods (baseline) and a second set that receives the rapid, low‐temperature annealing treatment immediately after deformation. Subject both sets to identical room-temperature tensile tests.
measurements: High-resolution microscopy to quantify microcrack density at the lamellar interfaces.
Room-temperature tensile tests to measure yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation (ductility).
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to assess interfacial bonding quality and check for any unintended microstructural coarsening.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the annealed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in microcrack density and improvement in tensile ductility without a concomitant drop in strength compared to the baseline samples.

The room temperature tensile test showed a fracture stress of 944 MPa and an elongation of 25.6%, from the engineering stress-strain curve given in Fig. 4a. These values converted to 1186 MPa and 22.8% in the true stress/strain condition. Noteworthily, this alloy exhibited an ultra-high strain hardening behavior, having the proof stress (the proof stress is determined by shifting the linear elastic curve to 0.2% strain. We choose to not to call it the yield stress, as the mechanism for such a low elastic limit is still unclear at this stage.) of 75 MPa but reaching the fracture stress close to 1.2 GPa. At elevated temperatures of 600 and 700°C (Fig. 4b), the proof stress, fracture stress and elongation were 95 MPa, 806 MPa, 33.7%, and 108 MPa, 538 MPa, 22.9%, respectively, both in the true stress/strain condition. The room-temperature strength of Al0.3CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys (HEAs) is relatively low owing to its intrinsic fcc structure. In the present study, the as-cast HEAs were subjected to cold rolling and subsequent annealing treatment (800, 900, and 1000 °C) to adjust the microstructures and tensile properties. This treatment process resulted in the partial recrystallization, full recrystallization, and grain coarsening with increasing the annealing temperature. It was found that the large and spherical B2 precipitates were generated in the recrystallized grain boundaries of three annealing states, while the small and elongated B2 precipitates were aligned along the deformation twins in the non-recrystallized region of the 800 °C-annealing state. The former B2 precipitates assisted in refining the recrystallized grains to quasi ultra-fine grain and fine grain regimes (with the grain sizes of ~0.9, ~2.2, and ~7.2 μm). The tensile results indicated that the decreased annealing temperature induced the gradual strengthening of this alloy but also maintained the ductility at the high levels. decision.trend: Early work with eutectic high‐entropy alloys established that a dual-phase lamellar microstructure (e.g., alternating soft fcc and hard B2 phases) can yield high strength and high ductility at room temperature. Subsequent studies refined these microstructures through thermomechanical processing—such as severe deformation and controlled annealing—to introduce ultrafine grains and hierarchical heterogeneities that improve work‐hardening and delay failure. However, while these treatments have maximized strength and activated crack‐arrest mechanisms, the intrinsic problem of microcrack initiation at numerous internal lamellar interfaces has not been directly overcome.
decision.unsolved: The fundamental unsolved issue is that the large number of internal boundaries within the dual‐phase lamellar colonies act as sites for microcrack nucleation under tensile deformation. Although previous strategies have improved overall properties, none have directly reinforced the integrity of the lamellar interfaces so as to prevent the crack initiation that limits room‐temperature ductility.
decision.lever: Implementing a short-duration, low‐temperature rapid annealing post‐deformation treatment aimed specifically at enhancing interfacial cohesion. This treatment would use a high heating rate and a precise temperature window that promotes localized interface diffusion and partial recrystallization along the lamellar boundaries without over-coarsening the microstructure.
decision.why: This intervention builds directly on the observed trend that controlled thermomechanical processing can refine and heterogenize eutectic microstructures for improved performance. By targeting the internal boundaries—with a short, tailored annealing step—it is possible to relieve residual interfacial stresses and enhance bonding at the phase interfaces. This should suppress microcrack initiation while preserving the high-strength lamellar architecture, thereby simultaneously improving both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility. An experiment that falsifies the hypothesis would be if the annealed samples show no reduction in microcrack density or even degraded ductility relative to a baseline processed solely by conventional deformation, under otherwise identical testing conditions.
